newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government gambles on truck strike crumbling.
newsitem.headline: French government gambles on truck strike crumbling.

text.p: France's embattled conservative government took a big gamble on Thursday when it ended mediation efforts in a truck drivers' strike that is choking the economy, declaring victory and urging the truckers to return to work.

"I consider (the mediator's) mission is a success. He has achieved a positive result. I would not understand it in these circumstances if the roads remained blocked," Transport Minister Bernard Pons told a hastily summoned news conference in the middle of the night after the talks collapsed.
The first reaction at 244 roadblocks across the country was a defiant "non" and a determination by all five trade unions to fight on for pay rises refused by road haulage employers.

The government appears to be counting on the 11-day blockade of provincial highways, ports, borders and fuel depots crumbling through a mixture of exhaustion, satisfaction at having won early retirement for drivers, and public pressure.

Officials seem to believe that other workers -- and many older truck drivers -- will see the achievement of retirement at 55 instead of 60 for truckers with 25 years' service, plus some concessions on working hours, as a fair outcome.
The mediator, Robert Cros, said he had invited both sides to the Transport Ministry on Friday to sign agreements reached in the talks, putting the onus on the unions to accept the package.
But the growing cost to the economy, Prime Minister Alain Juppe's deep unpopularity and public sympathy for the truckers mean the government is by no means assured of prevailing.

"The political bill is seriously mounting for Alain Juppe, who really didn't need this," said political commentator Michele Cotta. "The truckers' revolt underlines the improvisation with which this government handles even the most explosive issues."

By muddling through and trying to spin out the negotiations, the Juppe administration had merely enabled the truckers to tighten their stranglehold on the economy while the road haulage bosses let the government make all the concessions, she said.
"If the government was playing for time, it is about to lose. If it plans to use force now, that will be more difficult because there are so many obstacles to clear," Cotta said.
In 1992, the then Socialist government failed in a bid to use tanks to clear roadblocks by truckers striking over a points system for driving licences and was forced to back down.

More than half of the country's 147 fuel depots are now barricaded by trucks. About 2,000 of its 18,000 petrol stations have run out of fuel and government prefects in 25 out of 101 territorial districts have imposed rationing to keep priority vehicles such as ambulances, fire engines and buses on the road.

Factories that depend on supplies by road are having to halt production and France's biggest wholesale fresh food market at Rungis, in the southern Paris suburbs, is paralysed, alarming growers of fresh produce.
The strike is starting to cause economic side-effects in Britain, Spain, Portugal, Germany and Belgium. Several thousand foreign truck drivers are still stranded in France.
The government's main hope may reside in exploiting fatigue, cold weather and divisions between the unions.

While the Communist-led CGT is pushing for an all-out strike over pay, the pro-Socialist CFDT is keen to settle for a deal on retirement and shorter working hours, and the non-partisan Force Ouvriere is pleading witht the government to have one more go at mediation.
